results.summary: This design is intended to light up a number on a seven-segment display when a switch is pressed. The documentation is very thin: it only states that pressing the right switch should light the right number, and the pin names are generic inputs and outputs. It requires an external seven-segment display and switches, but no wiring details are given. The project appears to be a beginner exercise and provides no test procedure or implementation detail.

This project implements a simple counter built from flip-flops that increments when a pushbutton is pressed and shows the count on a seven-segment display. Testing consists of pressing the button and checking that the displayed number counts correctly. It needs an external pushbutton and a seven-segment display, and the documentation notes that the button may need a capacitor for debouncing. The design is a small educational exercise with no silicon results reported.

This is a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces a 5-bit sum output. The documentation is minimal, describing only the input and output widths and stating that it is a 4-bit adder. No external hardware is required, and testing is simply applying inputs and observing the sum. It is a basic educational arithmetic circuit with no further implementation details or silicon results.

This design implements AND, NAND and OR gates driven by two inputs, plus a clock divider using sixteen flip-flops with taps at the 12th and 16th stages. It is tested by setting the inputs and comparing the gate outputs against a truth table, and by observing the divided clock outputs flashing at different rates with a 10 kHz clock. No external hardware is required beyond the chip's pins. The project is explicitly a simple test of basic gates and clock division, likely a first Wokwi exercise.

This project appears to implement AND and NAND gates along with clock division by 12 and 16, based on its pin names. However, the documentation fields for how it works, how to test it, and external hardware all contain only the placeholder text 'some words'. There is not enough information to describe the design's behavior or intended use. It is likely a template or test project with no meaningful documentation.

This design is a 4-bit down counter built from four flip-flops that counts backward from 1111 to 0000 and then wraps around. It is tested by checking that the output counts downward from F to 0, and it is intended to drive an external seven-segment display. The documentation explains the counting sequence and bit ordering clearly, though the test description is informal. It is a straightforward educational counter with no reported silicon results.

This project was created to experiment with a DSR flip-flop, with two XOR inputs, a reset input and a data input, and two outputs labeled as the flip-flop's Q. Testing is done by setting the DIP switches to one or zero. No external hardware is listed, and the documentation is sparse, giving no detail on the flip-flop's behavior or the role of the XOR inputs. It is a small personal experiment rather than a complete application.

This design is meant to drive a seven-segment display by putting a high level on one of the inputs to activate individual segments. The documentation is very thin, with a one-line description in German and no real explanation of the mapping between inputs and segments. It requires an external seven-segment display, and testing is described only as using it for a seven-segment display. The pin names are generic and the project appears to be an unfinished template.

This project is titled as an extension of a running-light design, with eight inputs and eight outputs, but the documentation fields for how it works, how to test it, and external hardware all say only 'later'. There is no usable description of the design's function or behavior. It appears to be an unfinished student project with no meaningful documentation. No tags beyond its apparent LED running-light theme can be supported.

This project is a running-light design with four LED outputs, described in German as an extension of a running light. Testing consists of turning it on and watching the LEDs, and it requires external LEDs. The documentation is extremely brief and gives no detail on the pattern, timing or implementation. It appears to be a simple student exercise with no reported silicon results.
